title: What Percentage of Your Income Should Go to Savings at Different U.S. Age Groups
description: Benchmarking your savings rate from your 20s to your 60s.
content:
One of the most common questions financial planners receive is, 'Am I saving enough?' The answer depends entirely on your age. Saving 10% in your 20s is excellent, but saving 10% in your 50s (if you haven't started yet) is catastrophic. As you age, your 'Time Horizon' shrinks, meaning your 'Savings Rate' must increase to compensate for the lost years of compound interest. This guide provides specific percentage targets for every decade of life to ensure you land safely in retirement.

Key Takeaways

  • The 20s (The Habit Decade): Aim for 10-15%. The dollar amount is small, but the time multiplier is huge. Establishing the habit of living on less than you make is the primary goal.
  • The 30s (The Squeeze): Aim for 15-20%. Expenses peak (kids, homes), but income usually rises. Avoid lifestyle creep to keep the rate steady.
  • The 40s (The Peak): Aim for 20-25%. This is usually your highest earning decade. If you are behind, this is the time to aggressively catch up.
  • The 50s (The Sprint): Aim for 30%+. With kids leaving the nest and mortgages potentially paid down, divert that cash flow to 'Catch-Up Contributions'.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security replaces about 40% of pre-retirement income for average earners, but significantly less for high earners. The 'Savings Rate' is the only variable you control to fill the gap between Social Security and your lifestyle needs.

The Savings Rate Ladder

How the target shifts as the compounding window closes.

Age 20-29: Target 10-15%

The Math: $1 invested at 20 is worth ~$88 at 65.
Focus: Get the 401(k) match (free money) and start a Roth IRA. If you save 15% starting now, you can likely retire at 60 without stress.

Age 30-39: Target 15-20%

The Math: $1 invested at 30 is worth ~$28 at 65.
Focus: Fight 'Lifestyle Creep'. When you get a raise, bank 50% of it. Do not let your house and car payments consume your entire raise.

Age 40-49: Target 25%

The Math: $1 invested at 40 is worth ~$10 at 65.
Focus: You have to do more heavy lifting. Compounding is less effective. Max out your 401(k) ($23,000 limit).

Age 50+: Target 30-40%

The Math: $1 invested at 50 is worth ~$4 at 65.
Focus: Catch-Up Contributions. You can add an extra $7,500 to your 401(k) annually. Use it.

How to calculate your Rate

  1. The Formula: (Employee 401k + Employer Match + IRA + Cash Savings) / Gross Income.
  2. Example: You earn $100k. You put $10k in 401k. Employer puts $4k. You put $6k in IRA. Total = $20k. Savings Rate = 20%.
  3. The 'One Percent' Challenge: If you are behind, increase your rate by 1% every 3 months. You won't feel the pinch, but in 2 years, you will be saving 8% more.
  4. Principal Payments: Paying off mortgage principal counts toward 'Net Worth', but not 'Retirement Liquidity'. Count it as a separate tier of savings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 10% enough?

Only if you start at 22 and never stop. If you start at 30, 10% is likely too low to maintain your standard of living in retirement.

What if I can't save that much?

Start where you are. 5% is infinitely better than 0%. But be realistic: a low savings rate means a later retirement age (70+).

Does saving for a house count?

No. That is 'Deferred Spending'. Retirement savings is money you will never spend until you quit working.
